clue.text: Husband enters to wreck party

indicators.note: one piece entering another means it is placed inside it

parts.note: to trash something is to wreck it

explanation.surface: A spouse barges in and wrecks the festivities.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrash is informal British slang for a lively party or celebration.

clue.text: Extraordinarily powerful article Poirot was on to

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece that sits on another comes above it, so first in the answer

parts.note: Hercule is the first name of Agatha Christie's detective Poirot
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A powerful newspaper piece that the famous detective had cracked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was on to' looks like Poirot sniffing out a clue, but in this down clue it puts his first name above the article.
explanation.definitionFit: Herculean means needing or showing the great strength of Hercules, the mythical strongman.

clue.text: Old soldier heading off demonstrator

indicators.note: taking the head off means removing the opening letter of the word

parts.note: a marcher is a protester on a demonstration

explanation.surface: A veteran trooper intercepts a protester before trouble starts.
explanation.definitionFit: Archers were bowmen in old armies, so the word names a soldier of earlier times.

clue.text: Mischievous spirit to depart, limpin' around

indicators.note: the limping word goes round the departing word, enclosing it

parts.note: hobblin' is limping, with the dropped g kept by the clue's apostrophe
to go is to depart

explanation.surface: An impish sprite hobbles away on a bad leg.
explanation.definitionFit: A hobgoblin is a mischievous imp or sprite of English folklore.

clue.text: Largely woolly letter from abroad?

parts.note: the Greek letter's name is mostly made of the word for a woolly young sheep, with only two letters added

explanation.surface: A fuzzy, vague note posted from overseas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from abroad' points to a foreign (Greek) letter rather than a piece of post; 'Largely woolly' says most of its name is a lamb.
explanation.definitionFit: Lambda is the eleventh letter of the Greek alphabet, and its first four letters spell a sheep's young.

clue.text: Doctor taking holiday: that's a relief

definitions.text: Doctor taking holiday: that's a relief

parts.words: Doctor taking holiday: that's a relief
parts.note: when a GP goes away, a stand-in doctor relieves them, so this person is literally the relief

explanation.surface: A weary doctor sighs happily at finally getting a break.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a doctor or cleric who stands in temporarily while the regular one is away.

clue.text: Policemen in some unit reorganised

indicators.note: letters that are reorganised are put into a new order

explanation.surface: Officers in a squad that has been restructured.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reorganised' shuffles the eight letters of SOME and UNIT together.
explanation.definitionFit: Mounties are members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Canada's federal police force.

clue.text: Automobile seen in Kansas City

parts.note: the American car maker shares its name with a Wild West cow town in Kansas, the one Wyatt Earp policed

explanation.surface: A car spotted on the streets of a Midwestern city.
explanation.walkthrough: Kansas City is a real place, which makes the solver look for a car seen there; the trick is that the car is named in the other Kansas city, Dodge City.
explanation.definitionFit: Dodge is an American motor manufacturer, and Dodge City is a famous cow town in Kansas.

clue.text: Sort of pipe Spooner couldn't confuse!

definitions.text: Sort of pipe Spooner couldn't confuse!

parts.words: Sort of pipe Spooner couldn't confuse!
parts.note: a pipe made from a maize cob has two words both starting with the same letter, so swapping their first sounds leaves it unchanged

explanation.surface: A type of tobacco pipe whose name even the muddled Reverend Spooner could not mangle.
explanation.walkthrough: Spooner, the Oxford don famed for swapping the first sounds of words, would swap C for C here and say the same thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A corncob pipe has its bowl carved from a dried maize cob, the kind smoked by Popeye.

clue.text: Sphere in which your fortune may lie

definitions.text: Sphere in which your fortune may lie

parts.words: Sphere in which your fortune may lie
parts.note: a fortune teller gazes into a glass globe to read your future, and that reading might be untrue

explanation.surface: The field in which you could make your money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sphere' looks like a field of activity and 'fortune' like wealth; 'lie' hints the forecast may be false.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortune teller's glass globe is supposed to show the future to whoever gazes into it.

clue.text: Hint to politicians in the know

parts.note: a clue is a hint
the DUP is the Democratic Unionist Party of Northern Ireland

explanation.surface: Tipping off politicians who are already well informed.
explanation.definitionFit: Clued up is a British idiom for well informed about something.

clue.text: Unrealistic expectation of high tea?

parts.note: tea in the British sense of a meal, here one item served at it
something high is up in the sky

explanation.surface: An unlikely hope of a lavish early evening meal.
explanation.walkthrough: High tea is a British early evening meal with savoury food; the question mark warns that 'high' and 'tea' are to be read separately, the first giving the second half of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a promise or plan so improbable it will never be realised.

clue.text: Job done, cabbie, but now I'm confused

definitions.meaning: a taxi passenger arriving might say the driver has brought them to their destination
the phrase is also an admission of being stumped by a question

explanation.surface: A passenger thanks the taxi driver, then admits bewilderment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock admission that one has no answer, and literally thanks a driver for arriving.

clue.text: Level in cup match, right?

parts.note: a tie is a knockout match in a cup competition

explanation.surface: Asking whether the scores are equal in a cup game.
explanation.walkthrough: In British football a cup tie is a knockout match; 'Level' looks like an equal score but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A tier is one rank or layer in a stepped arrangement, such as seats in a stadium.

clue.text: Celtic fan, perhaps, sawing a leg off

indicators.note: something off is wrong or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A football supporter, perhaps, sawing off a limb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like part of 'sawing a leg off' but signals the anagram. Celtic is a Glasgow football club, so its fan may well be from Glasgow.
explanation.definitionFit: A Glaswegian is someone from Glasgow, home city of Celtic Football Club; 'perhaps' marks it as an example.

clue.text: Beach pebble or rock

parts.note: sand is what a beach is made of, so it stands for the beach
a pebble is a small stone

explanation.surface: Choosing between a pebble and a boulder on the shore.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandstone is a sedimentary rock made of compressed grains of sand.

clue.text: Copy restriction? Not at first

indicators.note: the word is used but not its first letter, which is dropped

parts.note: a limitation is a restriction

explanation.surface: A copyright limitation that did not apply at first.
explanation.definitionFit: An imitation is a copy or replica of something genuine.

clue.text: Nanny's nanny?

parts.note: a female goat is a nanny, and the person who looks after goats is like a nanny caring for children

explanation.surface: Asking who looks after the childminder.
explanation.definitionFit: A goatherd tends goats, including the female ones called nannies.

clue.text: Come ashore, admitting being a laird?

parts.note: to land is to come ashore
owning up means admitting, so owning can mean admitting

explanation.surface: Stepping off the boat and confessing to a Scottish title.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is a Scottish landed proprietor, so being one means owning an estate.

clue.text: School is excellent, but beginning to go bad

definitions.meaning: a ... school is a secondary school
... can mean excellent or superior, as in ... quality
meat or game that is ... is starting to smell off

explanation.surface: A school report: top marks now, but standards are slipping.
explanation.definitionFit: Three separate senses: secondary school type, superior quality, and gamey meat close to rotting.

clue.text: Put money in, having lost one's shirt?

definitions.meaning: to put money into a venture
split as two words, someone without a shirt is left wearing only a vest

explanation.surface: An investor who has lost everything after putting money in.
explanation.walkthrough: To lose one's shirt is an idiom for losing everything on a bet; the question mark tells you to take it literally. A vest is the British word for an undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: To invest is to commit money to a scheme in the hope of profit.

clue.text: Many thousands of moves taking ages

indicators.note: the letters move around into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Countless chess moves stretching a game out endlessly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'moves' rearranges all the letters of MANY THOUSANDS OF.
explanation.definitionFit: A month of Sundays is an idiom for a very long time.

clue.text: External route diverted

indicators.note: a diverted route goes a different way, so its letters take a different order

explanation.surface: A bypass road that has been rerouted.
explanation.definitionFit: Outer and external both mean situated on the outside.

clue.text: Start getting leg fixed

parts.note: in cricket the leg side is also called the on side
set means fixed or firmly in place

explanation.surface: Starting treatment by having a broken leg set.
explanation.definitionFit: An onset is the beginning of something, especially an illness.

clue.text: What children learn early: they can get through a door without opening it

definitions.meaning: children learn the ... of the alphabet early on

definitions.text: they can get through a door without opening it
definitions.meaning: post is pushed through the slot in a front door

explanation.surface: A riddle about something learnt young that slips through a closed door.
explanation.walkthrough: British front doors often have a letterbox slot, so post arrives without the door being opened.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both the characters of the alphabet and items of mail.

clue.text: An increasing problem ties boy in knots

indicators.note: something tied in knots is twisted up, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A growing worry that ties a lad up in knots.
explanation.definitionFit: Obesity is a health problem that is on the rise, and it literally makes people bigger.

clue.text: Believe this may be on the cards

definitions.meaning: to ... a story is to believe it

definitions.text: this may be on the cards
definitions.meaning: a card's ... limit is what you can spend on a ... card

explanation.surface: Believe it: this outcome is quite likely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the cards' is an idiom for likely, but here it means credit cards.
explanation.definitionFit: Credit is a verb for believing, and the money available on a credit card.

clue.text: Size of old temporary housing

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife
a tent is temporary shelter

explanation.surface: The dimensions of an old prefab shelter.
explanation.definitionFit: Extent means the size or scope of something.
